nameStory: Hairy lettuce gets its straightforward name from the fine hairs that cover its leaves and stem, giving the plant a soft, downy texture that's easy to feel. Like other wild lettuces, it belongs to the same family as garden lettuce, though you wouldn't want this bitter relative in your salad! The 'downy lettuce' nickname also refers to these soft hairs that make the plant feel fuzzy to the touch.
description: Hairy lettuce is a tall, lanky wildflower that can tower up to 6 feet high, making it one of our more impressive roadside plants. This biennial starts as a low rosette of leaves in its first year, then sends up a branching flower stalk in its second summer. The entire plant has a soft, fuzzy texture from tiny hairs covering the stems and leaves. Its small blue flowers cluster at the top of multiple branches, creating an airy, delicate appearance despite the plant's impressive height.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves feel noticeably soft and fuzzy due to fine hairs covering both surfaces, giving them a downy texture that's immediately apparent when touched

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small blue ray flowers (like tiny dandelions) appear in clusters at branch tips, with each flower head containing 12-24 blue petals and no center disc

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a tall, branching plant up to 6 feet high with multiple flowering branches creating an open, airy appearance at the top

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small brown seeds (achenes) with white fluffy parachutes that drift on the wind, similar to dandelion seeds but smaller

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Stem feels soft and hairy to the touch, and when broken releases a milky white sap typical of the lettuce family

habitat: Look for hairy lettuce in disturbed areas like roadsides, field edges, and woodland clearings where it can reach its full impressive height. It prefers areas with some sun but can tolerate partial shade, often growing along fence rows and in abandoned fields. This adaptable plant thrives in various soil types but seems to favor areas with decent drainage.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants appear as fuzzy-leaved rosettes close to the ground, already showing their characteristic soft, hairy texture.
seasonality.summer: Second-year plants shoot up their tall flowering stalks and bloom with clusters of small blue flowers from mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and disperse on fluffy white parachutes, while the tall brown stalks begin to dry and become more brittle.
seasonality.winter: Dead stalks may persist through winter as tall, dried brown stems that rattle in the wind before eventually breaking down.

funFact: Despite reaching heights of up to 6 feet, hairy lettuce spends its entire first year as just a small, ground-hugging rosette of fuzzy leaves, secretly building up energy in its taproot before making its dramatic vertical leap in year two!
confusionNotes: Hairy lettuce can be confused with other tall wild lettuces, but the soft, downy texture of its leaves sets it apart immediately—just give the leaves a gentle touch and you'll feel the difference. While prickly lettuce has spines along the leaf midrib, hairy lettuce feels soft and fuzzy all over.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you into thinking this is related to garden lettuce in any practical way—while they're botanical cousins, wild lettuces like this one are quite bitter and not considered edible. The milky sap that oozes from broken stems is also much more pronounced in wild species.
compareHints: Among New England's wild lettuces, hairy lettuce is the fuzziest—literally! While tall blue lettuce is smooth-leaved and prickly lettuce has actual spines, hairy lettuce feels soft and downy to the touch. Canada wild lettuce can also be tall but lacks the distinctive fuzzy texture that makes hairy lettuce immediately recognizable by feel.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the wild lettuces, tall blue lettuce stands out for its exceptional height and pale blue flowers - Canada wild lettuce has yellow blooms, while prickly lettuce has spiny leaves and is much shorter.
Canada wild lettuce differs from tall blue lettuce by its pale yellow flowers (versus blue), and from prickly lettuce by its smooth leaves without spines.
Prickly lettuce stands out from other wild lettuces by its prickly leaf undersides and the tendency for leaves to twist vertically.
Garden lettuce differs from its wild Lactuca relatives by having much broader, more tender leaves without the deeply cut or prickly edges found on species like prickly lettuce or Canada wild lettuce.
